query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under sustained high-temperature cyclic loading, an initially homogeneous high-entropy alloy experiences stress‐assisted, thermally activated local segregation at grain boundaries that triggers the formation of nanoscale intergranular phases with intrinsically brittle characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex single-phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to cyclic mechanical loading at an elevated temperature (e.g., around 700°C) under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (~700°C), cyclic loading (alternating tension-compression with amplitudes sufficient to activate diffusion without causing gross plastic deformation), and an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, applied for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical heterogeneities at grain boundaries manifesting as nanoscale intergranular precipitates formed via stress-assisted segregation.
generation.mechanism: Under high temperature and cyclic stress, atomic mobility is locally enhanced, allowing slight deviations from the high-entropy equilibrium at grain boundaries. This reduction in effective configurational entropy facilitates local ordering and phase separation, leading to the nucleation of brittle precipitates at the interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline maintained at room temperature or under static conditions, the treated samples are expected to exhibit measurable grain boundary segregation and formation of nanoscale brittle precipitates, alongside a perceptible reduction in fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: Samples that are either held at room temperature or subjected to high temperature without cyclic loading, conditions under which the original homogeneous microstructure and toughness are maintained.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to become operative only when both the temperature and the cyclic loading amplitude exceed critical thresholds; below these parameters (e.g., low temperature or static stress), the alloy should not develop significant intergranular segregation nor suffer toughness degradation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact thresholds for temperature, stress amplitude, and cyclic duration that drive the onset of noticeable segregation and phase formation are not precisely determined, and the kinetics of such transformations remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical alloy samples and subject one group to cyclic loading at ~700°C while keeping control groups either at room temperature under cyclic loading or at 700°C under static loading. After processing, perform microstructural analyses (e.g., atom probe tomography and TEM) of the grain boundaries and evaluate fracture toughness using standardized mechanical tests.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and evidence of segregation using atom probe tomography (APT)
Nanoscale precipitate characterization using transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Fracture toughness and overall mechanical performance via standardized tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature cyclic loading samples do not show statistically significant grain boundary segregation, the presence of nanoscale brittle precipitates, and a corresponding degradation in fracture toughness relative to control groups, then the hypothesis is falsified.
